title: Senate passes stopgap funding bill before shutdown deadline
summary: The Senate voted 60 to 38 on Friday night to pass a stopgap spending bill that funds the government at current levels through January 30, averting a shutdown at midnight. The bill includes $12 billion in disaster aid and now goes to President Mark Ellis, who the White House said would sign it on Saturday. Eleven Republicans joined most Democrats in supporting it, while 36 Republicans and two Democrats opposed it. Majority Leader John Doe said it keeps the lights on, while critics on both sides objected to its contents.

agreedFacts.fact: The Senate passed the stopgap spending bill 60 to 38 on Friday night, hours before a shutdown would have begun at midnight.
The bill funds the government at current levels through January 30.
The bill includes $12 billion in disaster aid for areas hit by this fall's hurricanes.
Eleven Republicans voted for the bill.
Thirty-six Republicans voted against the bill, along with Democratic Senators Paul Grant of Oregon and Lena Brooks of Vermont.
The bill goes to President Ellis, and the White House said he would sign it on Saturday.
Congress still has to reach a full-year funding deal after weeks of stalled talks, with the new deadline at the end of January.

disputed.claim: Whether the stopgap bill is an acceptable way to proceed

positions.position: Majority Leader John Doe said the bill is not one any of them would have written but that it keeps the lights on while negotiators work on full-year funding, and that a holiday shutdown would have hurt millions of families.
Sen. Mary Roe of Utah, who led opposition from the right, called it another kick of the can that adds to a debt children will pay, and said she would push for spending caps in January.
Democratic Senators Paul Grant and Lena Brooks voted no, saying the bill should have included an extension of expanded child care subsidies that expire at year's end.

disputed.claim: Whether the $12 billion in hurricane aid is adequate

positions.position: Democrats in affected states, including Sen. Ana Torres of Florida, said the $12 billion was inadequate, a down payment rather than a recovery plan, compared with the $38 billion governors requested. Torres still voted for the bill.
Other coverage reported the $12 billion figure without comment on whether it was sufficient.

disputed.claim: Border security funding and who is responsible for its absence from the bill

positions.position: Fox News reported the bill has no new border security money and that Democrats blocked a Republican amendment from Sen. Rick Hale that would have added $4 billion for border enforcement.
BBC News reported that Republicans demanded more border security money during budget talks while Democrats opposed cuts to social programmes.

framing.left: Mother Jones frames the bill as a shutdown averted but with unmet needs, stressing the shortfall in hurricane aid, food benefits for about 42 million people and expiring child care subsidies.
framing.center: The Hill and BBC News focus on the vote count, the deadline and the practical stakes, with the Hill adding the Senate floor debate and the BBC the impact on federal workers and holiday travel, and both noting the remaining fight over full-year funding.
framing.right: Fox News and The Daily Wire frame the bill as another punt on the spending fight, emphasizing conservative opposition, the 'kick the can' criticism, national debt and the lack of border security money.

recently: Budget talks stalled on November 18 as Republicans pressed for border security money and Democrats resisted cuts to domestic programs. On November 20 the House passed the stopgap through January 30 by 231 to 196, sending it to the Senate with a Friday midnight deadline.
